title: Orcas Smash Sunfish Like a Piñata — and Scientists Are Stunned
summary:
Have you ever hit a piñata at a birthday party? Now imagine a killer whale doing it — to a fish the size of a small car.

Scientists filmed orcas in the Gulf of California in 2024 and 2025. In both cases, one adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca slammed into it so hard the fish exploded into pieces.

Sharp-tail sunfish can grow up to 10 feet long. That's longer than a grown-up is tall!

Why would orcas do this? One idea: to break the huge fish into small bites for young orcas. After one explosion, a baby orca ate the little pieces. Another idea: it's just fun. Orcas are super social and clever, and they often play with their food.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist in New Zealand who watched the videos. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

Orcas already team up to hunt whales, knock penguins off ice, and even launch seals into the air. So smashing a sunfish? That's just another wild orca trick.
why_it_matters: It shows that even animals we have studied for years can still surprise us — and that watching carefully, like these scientists did, is how we learn new things about the natural world.

background_read: Orcas, also called killer whales, live in every ocean on Earth and often swim in family groups called pods; they are famous for clever hunting tricks, like working together to catch large whales.
The Gulf of California (the sea between Mexico's mainland and the long Baja California peninsula) is home to whales, dolphins, sea turtles and many kinds of fish.
Marianne Nyegaard, the scientist in the story, is a marine biologist based in New Zealand (a country in the South Pacific Ocean, southeast of Australia) who studies big ocean fish such as sunfish.

WHY: Scientists think the smashing may break the huge fish into small bites for young orcas, or that the orcas are simply playing with their food

perspectives.description: Marine biologist Marianne Nyegaard said she was 'absolutely gobsmacked' and called it the coolest thing she had ever seen.
One idea is that the orcas are being useful parents, breaking a giant fish into bite-size pieces that a baby orca can eat.
Another idea is that there is no deeper reason: orcas are social and clever and often play with their food, so smashing a sunfish may just be fun.
